Plot method for estimating contrasts

Source: R/plot.estimate_contrasts.R
plot.see_estimate_contrasts.Rd

The plot() method for the modelbased::estimate_contrasts() function.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'see_estimate_contrasts'
plot(x, data = NULL, show_data = FALSE, ...)

Arguments

x

An object.

data

The estimated means, obtained with modelbased::estimate_means().

show_data

Logical. If TRUE, the plot draws the raw data of the model as jittered points behind the lighthouses. The raw data come from insight::get_data() for the model stored in x, not from data. A response that is logical or a factor with two levels is drawn as 0 and 1, with TRUE or the second level as 1. A response log(y), log2(y), or log10(y), with y a column of the data, is drawn as the raw data of y if both the contrasts and the means were estimated with transform = TRUE. Means without the transform attribute, such as a plain data frame, then give an error. Ratio contrasts are drawn with the raw data. The plot stops with an error in these cases:

  • show_data is not a single TRUE or FALSE.

  • x is the output of data_plot(), or it does not carry its model, or the model data cannot be retrieved.

  • The response is a cbind() of successes and failures in a binomial model.

  • The model transforms the response, for example log(y), and the contrasts and means are not back-transformed log contrasts and means as above.

  • The predict of the contrasts or of the estimated means is not one of "prediction", "response", "expectation", "invlink(link)", and "inverse_link", for example predict = "link". Means without this information, such as a plain data frame, are taken to be on the same scale as the contrasts.

  • The model data lack the response or a contrasted or by variable.

  • The estimated means do not include each value in the data of the contrasted and by variables, or each combination of their values. For example, a numeric by variable has values that the means were not estimated at.

...

Arguments passed to or from other methods.

Value

A ggplot2-object.

Details

If you estimate the contrasts with by, the plot draws each contrast from the estimated means of its own by level. The plot then has one panel per level, or combination of levels, of the by variables. The estimated means must include the contrasted variables and the by variables, and no other variables that split their rows further. If the means have no row for the levels of a contrast, the plot does not draw that contrast and gives a warning.

If you contrast two or more variables jointly, for example with contrast = c("am", "cyl"), the x axis shows their combinations of levels, such as "auto, 4". The first variable changes slowest along the axis.

The plot takes the estimates from the column of the means that their coef_name attribute names. For means without this attribute, such as a plain data frame, it takes the first of the columns Median, Mean, MAP, Coefficient, Probability, Proportion, and Rate. If the means have none of these columns, the plot stops with an error.

Each lighthouse starts at the estimated mean of Level1 of a contrast. For a difference, the lighthouse at Level2 spans that mean minus the bounds of the confidence interval. Contrasts with a Ratio column, from comparison = ratio ~ pairwise, are ratios of the means, so the lighthouse at Level2 spans that mean divided by the bounds of the interval. If the interval of a ratio includes 0, the plot does not draw that contrast and gives a warning. The contrasts must have the columns CI_low and CI_high.

Contrasts estimated with transform = TRUE are back-transformed to the scale of the response. With the default backend, if the model response is log(y), log(y, base = b), log2(y), or log10(y), these contrasts are ratios of the back-transformed means, and the plot draws them as ratios. If insight::find_transformation() reports the transformation "identity", as it does for an untransformed response and for scale(y), the plot draws them as differences. For other transformations, such as sqrt(y), and for transformations that insight::find_transformation() does not recognize, the plot stops with an error. With backend = "emmeans", which sets transform = TRUE by default, the contrasts are differences of the back-transformed means, and the plot draws them as differences. The plot stops with an error for ratio contrasts estimated with transform = TRUE, because for a transformed response they are not ratios of the back-transformed means.

The contrasts and the means must be on the same scale. The plot stops with an error if both record a predict value and the two differ. The predict values "response", "inverse_link", and "invlink(link)" count as the same scale. The plot also stops with an error if both record a transform value and the two differ. If neither value is a transform function and insight::find_transformation() reports the transformation "identity", the plot does not stop. Contrasts and means estimated with the same transform function also differ, because modelbased records the function on the contrasts and transform = TRUE on the means, so the plot stops.

Interpreting Lighthouse Plots

Lighthouse plots display both estimated marginal means and the uncertainty around their pairwise differences (contrasts) in a single visual:

  • Means and Error Bars: The points and vertical line ranges display the estimated marginal means for each level along with their individual confidence intervals.

  • Lighthouse Beams (Projected Uncertainty): The shaded polygonal bands ("beams") represent the pairwise contrasts. A beam originates at the point estimate of a reference level and projects toward the comparison level. At the target level, the vertical span of the beam represents the confidence interval of the estimated difference, anchored at the reference mean.

  • Interpretation: The vertical span of the projected beam at the target level corresponds to the confidence interval of the estimated difference, evaluated relative to the reference point estimate. Intuitively, it answers: "If the reference level is at value Y, where do we expect the comparison level to be based on the estimated contrast?"

  • Reading Significance: Because the beam illustrates the confidence interval of the difference, zero difference corresponds to a horizontal line from the reference point. If both edges of the beam tilt in the same direction (both rising or both falling), the confidence interval does not include zero (the difference is statistically significant). If one edge rises while the other falls, the beam straddles the horizontal line, indicating that a difference of zero remains plausible.


Lighthouse plots of the two studies. In black, each condition's mean and 95% CI, identical in both panels. In grey, the beam: the 95% CI of the difference between B and A, cast from B. The dashed horizontal line, added here as a reading aid, makes it easier to see which way each edge tilts.

Examples

# \donttest{
library(modelbased)

model <- lm(Sepal.Width ~ Species, data = iris)
contrasts <- estimate_contrasts(model)
#> We selected `contrast=c("Species")`.
means <- estimate_means(model)
#> We selected `by=c("Species")`.
plot(contrasts, means)


# with the raw data as jittered points
plot(contrasts, means, show_data = TRUE)


# contrasts of `am` within each level of `cyl`, one panel per level
d <- mtcars
d$cyl <- factor(d$cyl)
d$am <- factor(d$am, labels = c("auto", "manual"))
model <- lm(mpg ~ cyl * am, data = d)
contrasts <- estimate_contrasts(model, contrast = "am", by = "cyl")
means <- estimate_means(model, by = c("cyl", "am"))
plot(contrasts, means)


# joint contrasts of `am` and `cyl`, on an axis of combined levels
contrasts <- estimate_contrasts(model, contrast = c("am", "cyl"))
plot(contrasts, means)

# }
